sections.html:
Danville is an independent city in Southside Virginia, on the Dan River against the North Carolina border. It covers about 43 square miles at an elevation of 531 feet, roughly 70 miles south of Lynchburg and 45 miles northeast of Greensboro along U.S. 29. No county government stands between you and city hall: the city itself bills real estate tax. Pittsylvania County lies to the north and Caswell County, North Carolina, to the south.

Population was 42,590 in 2020, with 41,647 estimated for 2025, down from 53,056 in 1990. That slow decline shapes what sellers meet. Some older houses draw few bidders, and the 2020 census counted 22,259 housing units, 14.6 percent of them vacant, with a rental vacancy rate of 10.7 percent.

Tobacco and cotton mills built much of Danville's older housing. Houses put up for that earlier wealth still define many streets, and Victorian and mill-era homes can need foundation, plumbing and wiring work that conventional buyers shy away from. The whole city was named one of Virginia's Most Endangered Historic Sites in 2007, which gives you a sense of how much old building stock there is.

Several recognized historic districts exist, including the Old West End, Tobacco Warehouse, Downtown Danville, Holbrook-Ross Street and North Main, plus Penn's Bottom on Main Street. Millionaire's Row on Main Street has large late nineteenth and early twentieth century mansions, and the River District downtown has old warehouses converted to offices, lofts, apartments and restaurants.

  • Find out whether your house sits inside a historic district before planning exterior changes.
  • Ask the city whether a tax abatement or relief program covers your parcel.
  • Collect permits for earlier renovations, because older houses often carry unpermitted work.

Manufacturing, healthcare and a casino resort make up much of the job base. Japan Tobacco International, Goodyear, Nestle and Morgan Olson operate here, Sovah Health runs the hospital, and Caesars Virginia opened in December 2024 on the old mill site after voters approved a casino referendum in 2020. Employers here can also leave: a Swedwood factory opened in 2008 and closed in December 2019.

Steady employers help buyers qualify for loans, but a house that needs work still struggles with financing. That is where a cash buyer fits.

sections.h2: Real estate tax rate and due dates
sections.html:
The city lists its real estate tax rate at $0.83 per $100 of assessed value. Rates and assessments run from July 1 through June 30 of the following year, so a new year can bring a new rate. Bills go out in two halves.

BillMailed byDue date
First halfNovember 5December 5
Second halfMay 5June 5

For questions, call the Real Estate office at 434-799-5120, at 427 Patton Street, Room 301, or Central Collections at 434-799-5125. Have the parcel ID or the owner's name on the July 1 deed ready, because staff will ask. The city also runs programs for elderly or disabled relief, land use and delinquent taxes.

Two items come due at a Danville closing: any real estate tax still unpaid and Virginia's grantor tax on the deed. A tax lien ranks ahead of other liens and stays attached until the city has been paid. Your sales agreement should state which side covers which part of the tax year, because the statute leaves that to the contract.

The grantor tax is 50 cents per $500 of the price. The seller normally pays it unless the contract says differently, and the clerk of court collects it when the deed is recorded.

  • Get the payoff for the current half-year installment before closing day.
  • Ask the Division of Central Collections whether delinquent balances show on the parcel.
  • Have your title company run a lien and judgment search.
  • Save copies of any city notices about code or utility charges.

U.S. 58 runs east and west through the main commercial district, with a bypass along the Danville Expressway, and U.S. 29 runs north and south. U.S. 360 connects the city with Richmond, and the U.S. 29 bypass is planned as future Interstate 785. Amtrak's Crescent stops at the 1899 station at 677 Craghead Street. Buyers coming from Greensboro or Lynchburg find the city easy to reach.

George Washington High School, Galileo Magnet High School and the Piedmont Governor's School for Mathematics, Science, and Technology are among the public schools. Boundaries change, so check zoning with the school division directly.

Many owners here hold a house that is older, empty or hard to finance. Typical cases are:

  • An inherited house where the heirs live out of state.
  • A vacant home that attracts code notices and vandalism.
  • A mill-era house with deferred maintenance and old wiring.
  • A rental with tenant turnover or unpaid rent.

A cash sale means selling as-is, choosing your own closing date and skipping showings. The offer depends on the condition and title of the house. We buy directly or bring a vetted cash buyer, and you can compare the result against listing.

sections.h2: Paperwork and calls before you sell
sections.html:
Keep a short folder: the deed, the latest tax bill, permits for earlier work and any city letters. Because the city bills your tax directly, the Real Estate office and Central Collections are the two places to start, and both answer by phone. Ask Central Collections what the next installment will be, and ask the Real Estate office whether the assessment matches what you know about the condition of the house.

Owners of historic-district houses should also ask the city whether exterior work needs approval, and whether past changes were permitted. A buyer paying cash may not care about a missing permit, but a title company or later lender might, so it is better to know before you sign.

sections.h2: Steps for a vacant or inherited house
sections.html:
Heirs usually begin by establishing who has authority to sign the deed. An attorney or title company can confirm that before you commit to anything. Next, gather the latest tax bill, any city notices and a list of what is wrong with the house. Call Central Collections to learn whether back taxes are owed, then ask the Real Estate office about the assessment if the figure looks off.

Once an offer is accepted, the title company searches for liens, prepares the deed and collects the grantor tax at recording. If a house has sat empty for a while, expect questions about utilities and code compliance, and answer them honestly. A buyer paying cash will price the repairs in, but unexpected surprises at closing can still slow things down.

faqs.q: What is the real estate tax rate in Danville, VA?
faqs.a: The city lists $0.83 per $100 of assessed value. Rates take effect July 1 and run through the next June 30, so check the city's Real Estate Taxes page for the current figure.

faqs.q: When are Danville property taxes due?
faqs.a: December 5 and June 5. The city mails the first-half bill by November 5 and the second-half bill by May 5.

faqs.q: Can I sell a vacant or inherited house in Danville?
faqs.a: Yes. Heirs can sell once the person with authority signs the deed, and a cash buyer can take the house as-is. Have an attorney or title company confirm that authority first.

faqs.q: Does Virginia charge a transfer tax on the seller?
faqs.a: A grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 of the price is charged on the deed. The seller usually pays, though the contract can shift some or all of it to the buyer.

faqs.q: Who do I call about Danville real estate tax amounts?
faqs.a: Central Collections at 434-799-5125, or the Real Estate office at 434-799-5120. Keep the parcel ID, address or tax bill in front of you.
